examples.label: Names, numbers and white space
examples.purpose: Three rules and two operators in one NFA: the scanner decides which rule a lexeme belongs to by where the DFA ends up.

examples.label: Keywords before names
examples.purpose: print is both a keyword and a name. It is listed first, so it wins where the two match the same lexeme; longer names still win.

examples.label: A rule that never matches
examples.purpose: With id first, print can never win: id matches every lexeme print does. The editor warns about the rule.

examples.label: < against <=
examples.purpose: After < the scanner reads one more character: = makes it <=, anything else is given back and < is returned.

examples.label: Integer and real literals
examples.purpose: After 1. the scanner needs a digit; without one it backs up to the integer 1 and starts again at the point.

examples.label: Optional fraction
examples.purpose: One rule with an optional part: the state after 12 accepts, so 12. is the number 12 followed by a stray point.

examples.label: Strings and comments
examples.purpose: [^"] and . match every character but a few, so characters no rule mentions fall in the class other and a string can hold anything.

examples.label: Names with underscores
examples.purpose: Letters, digits and the underscore overlap in two classes; the 63 characters become a few classes, however large the alphabet is.
